results.summary: This project is a deliberately useless test design created for a Tiny Tapeout Hackaday event. It has two inputs labeled a and b and eight outputs labeled 0 through 7, but the documentation states that it does not function and should not be used. There is no meaningful behavior to test, and the author notes that any disappointment is the user's own fault. The design serves only as a placeholder or joke submission.

This design converts a 4-bit binary-coded decimal input into the seven segment drive signals for a single common-cathode 7-segment display. It uses combinational logic gates to map input values 0 through 9 to the appropriate segment patterns. The design requires an external DIP switch for the BCD input and a common-cathode 7-segment display for output. A silicon test report confirms that the fabricated chip works as described.

This project contains a set of digital inverters of different sizes, along with a D flip-flop, intended for analog characterization on a digital Tiny Tapeout tile. Inputs and outputs are connected to the inverters, with some bidirectional pins allowing flexible configurations such as paralleling inverters or building an amplifier. Testing requires a signal generator and an oscilloscope to measure propagation delays and analog behavior. The design is notable for comparing digital inverter measurements with those from an analog tile, and it originated from a TT06 submission.

This design displays the letters 'E', 'F', 'A', and 'b' on a 7-segment display using a D flip-flop ring counter. It is controlled by input switches for run, reset, initial state selection, and blink control, and works best with a slow clock or manual stepping. The project is intended as a demonstration for the EFAB webinar and has been tested on silicon, with multiple reports confirming that it works as described. External hardware includes a 7-segment display and switches for input.

This project implements a 4-bit combination lock with a maximum of three unlock attempts and a master reset. The user sets a password, then enters attempts via input pins; after three failures the lock becomes locked until reset. External hardware such as buttons or switches is required for physical operation, and a microcontroller is recommended for admin reset control. Silicon testing confirms that setting the password, unlocking, and the lockout after three wrong attempts all function correctly.

This design is a hardware implementation of the Bivium-B stream cipher used as a non-linear feedback shift register (NLFSR). It includes a 177-bit NLFSR with feedback taps and an output function, and it provides eight outputs that expose internal register values for self-testing. The circuit can be initialized to all zeros and then run, with outputs compared against a Python simulation. External hardware such as a logic analyzer is needed to observe the outputs, and the design is notable for its use of a stream cipher as a PRNG.

This project is a simple 1-bit comparator that compares two input bits and indicates whether they are equal or which one is greater. It has two inputs (A and B) and three outputs: one for equality, one for A greater than B, and one for B greater than A. The design is purely combinational and can be tested by applying all four input combinations and observing the outputs, with LEDs recommended for visual indication. It is a basic educational logic circuit with no external hardware required beyond input switches and output LEDs.

This design is a hardware implementation of the Trivium stream cipher used as a non-linear feedback shift register (NLFSR). It contains a 288-bit NLFSR with three feedback taps and an output function, and it provides eight outputs that expose internal register values for self-testing. The circuit can be initialized to all zeros and then run, with outputs compared against a Python simulation. External hardware such as a logic analyzer is needed to observe the outputs, and the design is notable for its use of a stream cipher as a PRNG.

This design uses a chain of flip-flops to display the word 'HELP' on a 7-segment display, with each flip-flop representing one letter and the last one blanking all segments. It has only seven outputs for the segments and no inputs, so it simply shows the sequence after reset. The project is a minimal demonstration and has been tested on silicon, with the author confirming that it displayed 'HELP'. No external hardware is required beyond the 7-segment display.

This project attempts to recreate the decoding logic of the vintage HP 5082-7500 display, a custom ASIC from the 1970s, on modern silicon. The design is incomplete and currently does not work, as indicated by the title. It would require a 4-bit BCD input and an LED dot-matrix display for testing, but no functional behavior is documented. The project is notable only as an unfinished attempt to reproduce historical logic.
